styles.comments: Most sake finishes fermentation near 18–20% ABV — among the highest of any naturally fermented beverage, achieved by multiple parallel fermentation, in which koji enzymes saccharify starch at the same rate the yeast consumes the sugar — and is then cut with water to about 15–16%. Genshu omits that cut. Denser, warmer, more intense; often served over ice (on-za-rokku), which is one of the few sanctioned uses of dilution at the table.
styles.ingredients: As per the underlying grade.
styles.history: The dilution convention arose partly from tax structure and partly from the palate expectations of the domestic market.
styles.examples: Common in nama genshu seasonal releases

styles.name: Nigorizake (にごり酒) — Cloudy
styles.impression: Coarsely strained rather than clarified — white, textural, frequently sweet.
styles.comments: The legal requirement is that the mash be strained through *something*; the mesh may be coarse enough to leave substantial rice solids. That is the line between nigorizake, which is seishu, and doburoku, which is not strained at all and falls into a different tax class. Ranges from a light haze (usu-nigori) to a thick, spoonable suspension. If bottled active it may continue to ferment and build pressure — several producers ship deliberately sparkling nigori, and the bottles need careful opening.
styles.ingredients: As per the underlying grade.
styles.history: The visual ancestor of all sake; clear sake is the later refinement.

styles.name: Muroka (無濾過) — No Charcoal Filtration
styles.impression: Skips the activated-carbon polish, keeping colour and flavour that filtration would strip.
styles.comments: Conventional practice passes pressed sake over activated charcoal to remove colour and soften rough aromatics. Muroka omits it, leaving a faintly golden or greenish tint and a fuller, more assertive flavour. Frequently combined as muroka nama genshu — unfiltered, unpasteurised, undiluted — which is about as unmediated as commercial sake gets and is a hallmark of the modern jizake movement.
styles.ingredients: As per the underlying grade.
styles.history: Charcoal filtration became standard in the 20th century for cosmetic consistency; muroka is a deliberate reversal.

styles.name: Koshu / Jukusei-shu (古酒・熟成酒) — Aged Sake
styles.impression: Deliberately matured — amber to brown, with sherry, mushroom, caramel and soy notes.
styles.comments: There is no statutory minimum age for the term, though the Long-Term Aged Sake Producers Association applies a three-year convention for jukusei koshu. Ageing drives Maillard chemistry between amino acids and sugars, darkening the sake and building umami; warm-aged examples develop quickly and heavily, cold-aged ones more slowly and delicately. Junmai and kijōshu age best because they carry the amino acid load to work with. Sake is otherwise conventionally treated as a fresh product with a stated brewing year (BY) rather than a vintage.
styles.ingredients: As per the underlying grade.
styles.history: Aged sake was recorded in the Edo period, disappeared under the Meiji tax regime that charged duty at production, and returned from the 1970s.

styles.name: Sparkling Sake / Awasake (スパークリング清酒)
styles.impression: Carbonated sake, from lightly petillant nigori to bottle-fermented and disgorged.
styles.comments: Not a tax-law designation. The awasake Association applies a voluntary standard for the premium end: bottle-refermented, no added carbon dioxide, clear after disgorgement or fine filtration, minimum pressure, and made only from rice, koji and water. Below that sits a large market of low-alcohol force-carbonated products around 5–8% ABV. Bottle-conditioned nigori sits in between and is often actively fermenting in the bottle.
styles.ingredients: As per the underlying grade; secondary fermentation from residual or added sugar.
styles.history: The premium bottle-fermented category dates to the 2010s and the awasake standard to 2016.
styles.examples: Bottle-fermented awasake and commodity sparkling sake

styles.name: GI Nihonshu (日本酒) — 'Japanese Sake'
styles.impression: A national geographical indication: only sake made in Japan from Japanese rice may be called nihonshu.
styles.ingredients: Rice grown in Japan, rice koji made from Japanese rice, and water; the entire production — fermentation, pressing, filtration and bottling — carried out in Japan.
styles.comments: Designated by the National Tax Agency in December 2015. Sake brewed outside Japan, of which there is now a substantial quantity in the United States, Canada, France, Norway and elsewhere, remains legally seishu-equivalent in its own jurisdiction but cannot be labelled nihonshu for markets recognising the GI. The designation protects the word, not the method — a foreign brewer may use identical rice varieties, koji and technique.
styles.history: Part of a broader Japanese push to secure GI protection for its agricultural and beverage exports.
styles.examples: All Japan-produced sake meeting the conditions

styles.name: Regional Sake GIs (Yamagata, Hakusan, Nada, Harima…)
styles.impression: Prefectural and sub-regional designations, each with its own production specification and tasting panel.
styles.ingredients: Set by each individual GI specification — typically prescribing local water, permitted rice, production within the delimited area, and a sensory approval step.
styles.comments: GI Hakusan (Ishikawa, 2005) was the first, followed by GI Yamagata (2016) — the first covering an entire prefecture — and subsequently Nada Gogo (Hyogo), Harima, Mie, Nagano, Toyama, Saga, Yamanashi and others. Specifications commonly require that the rice and water be local, that the sake be brewed and bottled within the area, and that it pass an organoleptic assessment before the designation may be used. Because each is distinct, the GI on a label tells you the sake met a regional committee's standard, not that it belongs to a defined flavour category.
styles.history: Modelled on European wine appellation practice and administered by the National Tax Agency.
styles.examples: GI Yamagata, GI Hakusan, GI Nada Gogo

styles.name: Doburoku (どぶろく) — Unstrained Rice Brew
styles.impression: The unstrained ancestor of sake — thick, porridge-like, actively fermenting, and legally not sake at all.
styles.ingredients: Rice, rice koji and water, fermented and consumed without pressing or straining.
styles.comments: Because it is never filtered it falls outside the seishu definition and is taxed as 'other brewed liquor' (その他の醸造酒). Home production remains illegal in Japan, but designated doburoku tokku — special deregulation zones established from 2002 — allow licensed farm and inn producers to make and sell it, which has driven a rural revival. Typically served fresh, sweet-sour and lightly effervescent.
styles.history: The pre-modern village and shrine brew; suppressed as home brewing was criminalised under the Meiji tax regime.
styles.examples: Farm-inn doburoku from deregulation zones; shrine festival brews

styles.name: Amazake (甘酒) — Non-Alcoholic Koji Drink
styles.impression: Saccharified rice without fermentation — sweet, thick, and useful to brewers as a koji reference point.
styles.ingredients: Rice and rice koji held warm (around 55–60 °C) until amylases convert the starch to glucose; or, in the cheaper version, sake lees plus sugar and water.
styles.comments: Included here because it isolates the enzymatic half of sake production. Holding koji at 55–60 °C runs saccharification without yeast — the mash goes sweet and stops. It demonstrates why sake reaches such high alcohol: in the real mash the same enzymes run continuously alongside the yeast, feeding it sugar slowly enough that it is never osmotically shocked. The koji-only version is alcohol-free; the sake-lees version carries residual alcohol, typically under 1%.
styles.history: Recorded in the Nihon Shoki as amanotamuzake; a traditional summer restorative and New Year drink.

legalStandards.title: Spirits: Legal Definitions & Standards of Identity
legalStandards.attribution: Unlike beer, mead, and cider, distilled spirits have no judging style guidelines — but they do have binding legal definitions. This edition compiles the actual statutory standards of identity: the Scotch Whisky Regulations 2009 (UK), the Irish Whiskey Technical File, US 27 CFR Part 5 (TTB), EU Regulation 2019/787, Mexico's NOM-006/NOM-070, French AOC decrees, and equivalent national standards. Figures are the legal minima/maxima, not sensory targets. Compiled for reference; always check the current regulation for the jurisdiction you are producing in.

styles.name: Single Malt Scotch Whisky
styles.impression: Whisky distilled at a single Scottish distillery from 100% malted barley in pot stills, matured in Scotland in oak.
styles.ingredients: Water, malted barley only. No other cereals. Yeast; fermentation by endogenous enzyme systems only.
styles.comments: Scotch Whisky Regulations 2009: distilled below 94.8% ABV; matured in oak casks not exceeding 700 litres, in Scotland, for at least 3 years; bottled at no less than 40% ABV. The only permitted additions are water and plain caramel colouring (E150A). Age statements must refer to the youngest whisky in the bottle.
styles.history: Protected UK geographical indication; the modern legal framework dates to the 1988 Scotch Whisky Act, consolidated in the 2009 Regulations.

styles.name: Single Grain Scotch Whisky
styles.impression: Scotch distilled at a single distillery from malted barley plus other whole cereals, typically in continuous column stills.
styles.ingredients: Water, malted barley, and whole grains of other cereals (commonly wheat or maize).
styles.comments: Same core Scotch Whisky Regulations 2009 requirements as single malt — <94.8% ABV off the still, ≥3 years in oak ≤700 L in Scotland, ≥40% ABV bottling. 'Single' denotes one distillery, not one cask or one grain.

styles.name: Blended Scotch Whisky
styles.impression: A blend of one or more single malt Scotch whiskies with one or more single grain Scotch whiskies.
styles.comments: The dominant Scotch category by volume. All component whiskies must independently meet the Scotch Whisky Regulations 2009. Blended Malt = malts only from multiple distilleries; Blended Grain = grains only from multiple distilleries.
styles.examples: Johnnie Walker, Chivas Regal, Famous Grouse

styles.name: Irish Whiskey
styles.impression: Whiskey distilled and matured on the island of Ireland; often triple-distilled and comparatively light.
styles.ingredients: Cereal grains; malted barley providing the enzymes.
styles.comments: Irish Whiskey Technical File (EU GI): distilled to less than 94.8% ABV; matured in wooden casks not exceeding 700 litres for at least 3 years on the island of Ireland; bottled at ≥40% ABV. Only water and plain caramel may be added.
styles.history: Protected EU geographical indication covering both the Republic of Ireland and Northern Ireland.

styles.name: Single Pot Still Irish Whiskey
styles.impression: The distinctive Irish style: a mixed mash of malted and unmalted barley pot-distilled at a single distillery, giving a characteristic creamy, spicy texture.
styles.ingredients: A mash of at least 30% malted barley and at least 30% unmalted barley; up to 5% other cereals permitted.
styles.comments: Defined in the Irish Whiskey Technical File. The unmalted barley — historically a response to 19th-century malt taxation — is what produces the category's signature mouthfeel.
styles.examples: Redbreast, Green Spot, Powers John's Lane

styles.name: Canadian Whisky
styles.impression: Whisky mashed, distilled and matured in Canada; historically rye-influenced and often light-bodied.
styles.comments: Canadian Food and Drug Regulations (B.02.020): mashed, distilled and aged in Canada; aged at least 3 years in small wood (≤700 L); bottled at ≥40% ABV. Uniquely, caramel and flavouring may be added — and up to 9.09% of another spirit may be blended in (the '9.09% rule'), which is why some Canadian whisky contains a small proportion of US bourbon or wine spirit.
styles.comparison: Often labelled 'rye' in Canada regardless of actual rye content, unlike US rye whiskey which requires ≥51% rye.

styles.name: Japanese Whisky
styles.impression: Whisky made in Japan, historically modelled on Scotch practice.
styles.comments: Japan had no binding legal definition until the Japan Spirits & Liqueurs Makers Association standard took effect in 2021 (voluntary, industry self-regulation): malted grain must be used, water must be extracted in Japan, saccharification/fermentation/distillation must occur at a Japanese distillery, distillation below 95% ABV, maturation ≥3 years in wooden casks ≤700 L in Japan, and bottling in Japan at ≥40% ABV. Products not meeting this may still legally be sold as Japanese-made whisky, so labels warrant scrutiny.

styles.name: Bourbon Whiskey
styles.impression: America's flagship whiskey: corn-dominant, aged in new charred oak, sweet and full.
styles.ingredients: Fermented mash of not less than 51% corn.
styles.comments: 27 CFR 5.143: distilled to no more than 80% ABV (160 proof); entered into the barrel at no more than 62.5% ABV (125 proof); stored in NEW charred oak containers; bottled at no less than 40% ABV (80 proof). No colouring, flavouring or other blending materials may be added. There is no minimum ageing period for plain 'bourbon' — but see Straight Bourbon.
styles.history: Bourbon may be produced anywhere in the United States, not only Kentucky — a common misconception.
styles.examples: Buffalo Trace, Maker's Mark, Wild Turkey

styles.name: Straight Bourbon Whiskey
styles.impression: Bourbon that has met a minimum maturation period.
styles.comments: All bourbon requirements plus storage in new charred oak for at least 2 years. If aged less than 4 years, the label must carry an age statement. 'Bottled in Bond' is stricter still (Standards of Fill / 27 CFR 5.88): the product of one distillation season by one distiller at one distillery, aged ≥4 years in a federally bonded warehouse, and bottled at exactly 50% ABV (100 proof).
styles.examples: Knob Creek, Elijah Craig, Henry McKenna Bottled-in-Bond

styles.name: Rye Whiskey (US)
styles.impression: Spicier, drier counterpart to bourbon.
styles.ingredients: Fermented mash of not less than 51% rye.
styles.comments: Identical distillation, barrel-entry and bottling limits to bourbon (≤80% ABV distillation, ≤62.5% ABV barrel entry, new charred oak, ≥40% ABV bottling). 'Straight Rye' requires ≥2 years.
styles.comparison: Contrast Canadian 'rye', which carries no rye-content requirement.

styles.name: Corn Whiskey
styles.impression: The legal ancestor of 'moonshine' — a corn-dominant whiskey that need not see new charred oak.
styles.ingredients: Fermented mash of not less than 80% corn.
styles.comments: 27 CFR 5.143: distilled to ≤80% ABV. Uniquely, if aged at all it must be in UNUSED uncharred oak or USED barrels, and entered at ≤62.5% ABV. It may also be sold unaged. This is the category most 'white whiskey' and commercial 'moonshine' is legally bottled under.
styles.comparison: 'Moonshine' is not itself a federal standard of identity. Commercially it is sold either as corn whiskey, as unaged whisky, or — if distilled above 95% ABV from sugar — as neutral spirits or a specialty/flavoured product.

styles.name: Tennessee Whiskey
styles.impression: Bourbon-spec whiskey charcoal-mellowed before barrelling.
styles.comments: Tennessee Code § 57-2-106 and the NAFTA/USMCA designation: must meet all bourbon requirements, be produced in Tennessee, and be filtered through maple charcoal before ageing — the Lincoln County Process. Prichard's holds a statutory exemption from the charcoal step.

styles.name: American Single Malt Whiskey
styles.impression: The newest US standard of identity: 100% malted barley from a single American distillery.
styles.ingredients: 100% malted barley.
styles.comments: Formalised by TTB in 2024 (27 CFR 5.144): mashed, distilled and matured in the United States at a single distillery; distilled to ≤80% ABV; matured in oak casks ≤700 L; bottled at ≥40% ABV. Unlike bourbon, the oak need not be new or charred.

styles.name: Rum (US standard)
styles.impression: Spirit from sugarcane products, ranging from light and clean to heavy and estery.
styles.ingredients: Sugarcane products — molasses, cane syrup, or cane juice.
styles.comments: 27 CFR 5.143: distilled from fermented sugarcane products at less than 95% ABV (190 proof) in such a manner that it possesses the taste, aroma and characteristics generally attributed to rum; bottled at ≥40% ABV. US law imposes no ageing requirement and no maximum congener limits, which is why 'rum' spans an enormous stylistic range.

styles.name: Rum (EU standard)
styles.impression: EU-regulated cane spirit with tighter congener requirements than the US definition.
styles.comments: EU Regulation 2019/787 Annex I(1): produced exclusively from molasses, cane syrup or cane juice; distilled at less than 96% ABV; minimum 225 g/hL of volatile substances at 100% ABV (a congener floor the US lacks); minimum 37.5% ABV. No added ethanol; sweetening only for rounding-off.
styles.comparison: The congener minimum means an EU 'rum' cannot be as neutral as some US-market products.

styles.name: Rhum Agricole (AOC Martinique)
styles.impression: Grassy, vegetal cane spirit distilled from fresh juice rather than molasses.
styles.ingredients: Fresh sugarcane juice only — never molasses.
styles.comments: AOC Martinique (1996): designated parcels on Martinique, specified cane varieties, fermentation without additives, single-column creole distillation to 65–75% ABV, bottled at ≥40%. Blanc rested ≥3 months; Élevé sous bois ≥12 months in oak; Vieux ≥3 years in oak ≤650 L.
styles.history: The style arose when 19th-century beet-sugar competition left cane juice available for direct distillation.

styles.name: Cachaça
styles.impression: Brazil's national spirit — fresh cane juice distilled to a comparatively low strength, retaining fruity and grassy character.
styles.ingredients: Fermented fresh sugarcane juice.
styles.comments: Brazilian Decree 6.871/2009 and MAPA Instruction 13/2005: produced in Brazil; distilled to 38–48% ABV (note the low maximum, which preserves congeners); up to 6 g/L sugar, or up to 30 g/L if labelled 'adoçada' (sweetened). Recognised as a distinctive product of Brazil by the US since 2013.

styles.name: Tequila
styles.impression: Cooked-agave spirit from designated Mexican regions, ranging from bright and peppery to oak-rounded.
styles.ingredients: Agave tequilana Weber, blue variety. '100% de agave' uses only agave sugars; 'mixto' permits up to 49% non-agave sugars.
styles.comments: NOM-006-SCFI-2012 and the Denominación de Origen: may be produced only in Jalisco and designated municipalities of Guanajuato, Michoacán, Nayarit and Tamaulipas. Bottled at 35–55% ABV. Classes by ageing: Blanco (unaged or <2 months), Joven/Oro (blended or lightly aged), Reposado (≥2 months in oak), Añejo (≥1 year in oak ≤600 L), Extra Añejo (≥3 years).

styles.name: Mezcal
styles.impression: Agave spirit traditionally roasted in earthen pits, typically smoky and highly variable by species and maker.
styles.ingredients: Any agave species permitted by the standard — espadín, tobalá, tepeztate, madrecuishe and many others — not restricted to blue Weber.
styles.comments: NOM-070-SCFI-2016: produced in designated states including Oaxaca, Guerrero, Durango, San Luis Potosí, Zacatecas, Michoacán, Puebla, Guanajuato and Tamaulipas. Bottled 35–55% ABV, always 100% agave. Three production classes: Mezcal (industrial methods permitted), Mezcal Artesanal (pit roasting, stone/wood milling, wood or clay stills), and Mezcal Ancestral (clay pot stills, most traditional throughout).
styles.comparison: All tequila is technically a mezcal in the historical sense, but the two now hold separate denominations of origin.

styles.name: Raicilla & Bacanora
styles.impression: Regional Mexican agave spirits with their own denominations of origin.
styles.comments: Bacanora (NOM-168, Sonora, from Agave angustifolia/pacífica) and Raicilla (DO granted 2019, Jalisco/Nayarit, from Agave maximiliana and others) were long produced informally — bacanora was outright prohibited in Sonora from 1915 to 1992 — and are now legally protected categories.

styles.name: Cognac
styles.impression: Double-distilled French grape brandy of great finesse, oak-matured.
styles.ingredients: Predominantly Ugni Blanc, with Folle Blanche and Colombard permitted.
styles.comments: AOC Cognac: grapes grown and distilled within the Charente/Charente-Maritime crus; double distillation in a copper alambic charentais, off the still at no more than 72.4% ABV; matured in French oak; bottled at ≥40% ABV. Age grades count from 1 April following harvest: VS ≥2 years, VSOP ≥4 years, Napoléon ≥6 years, XO ≥10 years (raised from 6 in 2018).

styles.name: Armagnac
styles.impression: Gascon grape brandy, typically column-distilled once and more rustic and aromatic than Cognac.
styles.comments: AOC Armagnac (Bas-Armagnac, Ténarèze, Haut-Armagnac): usually continuous distillation in the alambic armagnacais to a lower strength than Cognac, retaining more congeners; aged in Gascon or Limousin oak; ≥40% ABV. Vintage (millésime) bottlings are a far more common tradition than in Cognac.

styles.name: Calvados
styles.impression: Norman apple (and pear) brandy.
styles.ingredients: Cider apples, and up to 30% pears depending on the appellation.
styles.comments: Three AOCs: Calvados, Calvados Pays d'Auge (double pot distillation, ≥2 years) and Calvados Domfrontais (≥30% pears, column distillation, ≥3 years). Base cider fermented without added sugar; minimum 2 years in oak; ≥40% ABV.

styles.name: Pisco
styles.impression: Aromatic grape spirit from Peru or Chile — two distinct, legally separate products.
styles.comments: Peru (NTP 211.001): from eight permitted grape varieties in designated coastal regions; distilled to bottling strength with NO water added afterwards, no ageing in wood permitted (rest in inert vessels ≥3 months), 38–48% ABV. Chile's DO permits water reduction and oak. The two nations dispute the name internationally.
styles.examples: Barsol, Macchu Pisco (Peru); Alto del Carmen (Chile)

styles.name: Grappa & Pomace Brandy
styles.impression: Spirit distilled from grape pomace — skins, seeds and stems left after winemaking.
styles.comments: EU Regulation 2019/787: 'Grappa' is reserved for pomace of grapes produced and distilled in Italy (with parallel protections for Grappa di Ticino, Marc de Champagne, Bagaceira, Orujo, Tsipouro/Tsikoudia). Distilled at less than 86% ABV; ≥37.5% ABV bottling.

styles.name: Fruit Brandy / Eau-de-Vie
styles.impression: Unaged or lightly aged spirit distilled from whole fruit, prized for varietal aroma.
styles.comments: EU 2019/787: fermented from fruit flesh (with stones where traditional); distilled at less than 86% ABV; no added alcohol, colouring or flavouring; ≥37.5% ABV. Protected examples include Kirsch, Mirabelle, Poire Williams, Slivovitz and Calvados' cousins. US law defines a parallel 'fruit brandy' at ≥40% ABV.

styles.name: Gin
styles.impression: Neutral spirit flavoured with juniper as the dominant character.
styles.ingredients: Ethyl alcohol of agricultural origin plus juniper berries (Juniperus communis); other botanicals at the producer's discretion.
styles.comments: EU 2019/787 sets three tiers: 'Gin' (flavouring may be by any means, juniper predominant, ≥37.5% ABV); 'Distilled Gin' (redistilled with botanicals); and 'London Gin' (all flavour from redistillation of ethanol at ≥96% ABV with natural botanicals, no added colouring, sweetening ≤0.1 g/L, nothing added but water). US requires ≥40% ABV. Note that 'London Gin' is a method, not a place — it need not be made in London.

styles.name: Vodka
styles.impression: Spirit deliberately refined toward neutrality.
styles.comments: EU 2019/787: ethanol of agricultural origin rectified so as to selectively reduce the organoleptic characteristics of the raw material; ≥37.5% ABV. US 27 CFR: treated with charcoal or otherwise so as to be without distinctive character, aroma, taste or colour; ≥40% ABV. The EU permits raw-material labelling; if made from anything other than cereals or potatoes, the base must be declared.

styles.name: Absinthe
styles.impression: High-strength anise and wormwood spirit, traditionally louching when diluted.
styles.ingredients: Grande wormwood (Artemisia absinthium), green anise, and fennel — the 'holy trinity'.
styles.comments: Absinthe has no harmonised EU spirit-category definition; it is regulated through thujone limits — EU: ≤35 mg/kg in bitter spirits; US TTB: 'thujone-free' meaning <10 ppm, and the label may not depict hallucinogenic or psychotropic effects. Switzerland's Absinthe/Fée Verte du Val-de-Travers holds a protected geographical indication. Typical bottling strength 45–74% ABV.
styles.history: Banned across much of Europe and the US in the early 20th century; legalised again in the EU from the 1990s and in the US in 2007.

styles.name: Aquavit / Akvavit
styles.impression: Scandinavian spirit dominated by caraway or dill.
styles.comments: EU 2019/787: spirit drink flavoured with caraway seeds and/or dill seeds, distilled with botanicals; ≥37.5% ABV. Essential oils of other botanicals may contribute but caraway/dill must predominate. Norwegian Linie aquavit is traditionally matured in sherry casks shipped across the equator and back.

styles.name: Liqueur / Cordial
styles.impression: Sweetened flavoured spirit.
styles.comments: EU 2019/787: minimum 100 g/L sugar (lower thresholds for cherry and gentian liqueurs); ≥15% ABV. US 27 CFR: 'cordial/liqueur' requires ≥2.5% sugar by weight and flavouring from natural materials; ≥30 proof (15% ABV). Crème de cassis requires ≥400 g/L sugar in the EU.

styles.name: Baijiu
styles.impression: China's national spirit and the world's most-consumed by volume — solid-state fermented grain spirit with intense, distinctive aromatics.
styles.ingredients: Sorghum most typically, often with rice, glutinous rice, wheat or corn; saccharified and fermented by qū (麴) starter cultures carrying moulds, yeasts and bacteria.
styles.comments: Governed by Chinese GB/T national standards, which classify baijiu by aroma type (香型) rather than by region: strong/thick aroma (nóngxiāng), light aroma (qīngxiāng), sauce aroma (jiàngxiāng), rice aroma (mǐxiāng) and around a dozen others. Solid-state fermentation in earthen pits or stone vessels distinguishes it from nearly all Western spirits.

styles.name: Shochu & Awamori
styles.impression: Japanese distilled spirit, typically single-distilled and lower in strength than Western spirits.
styles.ingredients: Barley (mugi), sweet potato (imo), rice (kome), buckwheat or brown sugar; saccharified with kōji mould.
styles.comments: Japanese Liquor Tax Act distinguishes honkaku (single-distilled, 'authentic', ≤45% ABV) from korui (multiply-distilled, ≤36% ABV). Awamori is the Okinawan variant, made from long-grain Thai indica rice with black kōji (Aspergillus luchuensis); aged awamori is called kūsū.

styles.name: Soju
styles.impression: Korea's dominant spirit; modern mass-market soju is diluted and lightly sweetened.
styles.comments: Korean Liquor Tax Act separates distilled soju (증류식, from grain, retaining congeners) from diluted soju (희석식, neutral spirit cut with water and flavourings) — the latter accounts for the overwhelming majority of sales, typically bottled at 16–25% ABV. Traditional Andong soju is distilled and considerably stronger.

styles.name: Arrack, Feni & Palm Spirits
styles.impression: South and Southeast Asian spirits from palm sap, cashew apple or cane.
styles.comments: Ceylon Arrack is distilled from fermented coconut palm flower sap and is protected as a Sri Lankan product. Feni holds a Goan GI: cashew feni from cashew-apple juice, coconut feni from palm toddy, traditionally triple-distilled in earthen pots. Batavia arrack (Java) is cane-based with red rice cakes added to fermentation.

styles.name: Unaged Grain Spirit / 'Moonshine'
styles.impression: Clear, unaged spirit from a grain or sugar wash — the untaxed tradition, now sold legally under existing categories.
styles.comments: 'Moonshine' is a cultural term, not a US standard of identity. To be labelled legally a product must fall into an existing class: Corn Whiskey (≥80% corn, ≤80% ABV distillation, unaged or in used/uncharred oak); unaged 'whisky' generally (grain mash, <95% ABV); Neutral Spirits/Vodka if distilled ≥95% ABV; or a 'Distilled Spirits Specialty' if sugar-based or flavoured. Historically the term denotes illicit, untaxed production — which remains a federal offence regardless of the recipe.
styles.comparison: Sugar-wash 'moonshine' cannot legally be called whiskey at all, since whiskey requires a grain mash.
styles.examples: Ole Smoky, Sugarlands (sold as corn whiskey or specialty)
styles.tags: moonshine, white dog, unaged, corn whiskey
